source_document.body:
Anyone who has managed drivers knows that communication is rarely clean, even in the best of times. In a post-Montgomery liability environment, a late load, a tired driver or a casual text can become evidence. For freight brokers, whose business runs on relationships and fast decisions, the question is how to stay responsive without creating legal exposure.
That question is now landing on the desks of chief legal officers at some of the industry’s largest brokerages. At the FreightWaves Brokerage Compliance Symposium at F3, Aqil Naeem, co-founder and CEO of E3 Group , described how those conversations shaped the company’s products. E3 has built what Naeem describes as the biggest driver verification platform, and now one of the biggest driver communication platforms.
“These conversations stem from our conversations with many of the chief legal officers at the many top 20 brokers that we work with,” Naeem said. Those legal leaders came to E3 with an open question about how to handle driver communication when a single slip could carry exposure in the hundreds of millions. It became a core product issue and a standing topic with every customer: “how should you be talking to drivers in a safe way that doesn’t lead to a lawsuit.”
Where Courts Draw the Line
The risk doesn’t come from routine contact. According to Naeem, courts focus on a narrower question of whether a broker’s language shaped what the driver did.
“What courts really focus on are not people doing regular check-ins, etc. They have this doctrine about exercising agency over the driver,” Naeem said. Asking whether a driver is on track is one thing. Adding a reference to a $10,000 or $15,000 fine is another, even when the fine is accurate. “By mentioning a fine to someone, for example, even though it may be factual, that is a greater indication of exercising agency over what that driver is doing.”
The same logic applies on the verification side. Naeem pointed to a court case in which a broker was found liable for failing to verify that its carrier hadn’t double brokered the freight. Because the broker hadn’t done a simple check that the person picking up the load was who it should have been, it was held responsible.
His conclusion: “It really comes down to how extensive your SOPs are and gearing your SOPs around doing your minimum job as a freight broker, i.e., validating who’s picking it up, making sure they’re on time, and communicating what’s happening with that load, as opposed to exercising too much control over that load.”
Two Camps, No Consensus
Brokers have responded in very different ways. Naeem sees two ends of the spectrum. Some brokers want little to no contact with drivers, and some E3 customers have asked to hide data in the verification product to limit what they can see. At the other end are brokers with long SOPs designed to catch every contingency. “A lot of them are ironically going to these like 20 question SOPs,” he said, with every driver contact turning into a health and safety checklist.
Neither approach settles the hardest scenarios. If a driver reports being sick and the broker escalates to the dispatcher, who then fails to replace the driver, could a court find the broker negligent for not sourcing another carrier with eight hours of lead time? Naeem noted that opinions in court tend to run against brokers, because a broker looks like a large company with deep pockets rather than a business operating on thin margins.
His assessment was candid: “there is no right answer in terms of how you should be handling things it’s really just a function of becoming aware of them.”
Operations teams face a related dilemma when a driver says they’re low on hours or too tired to make delivery. Asking about a backup driver could be read as pressure to keep driving. Resetting the appointment and absorbing the customer fallout carries its own cost. “You just have to pick the kind of poison that you’re willing to live with,” Naeem said, adding that the right call may vary by customer, since some have stricter delivery requirements than others.
Low-Hanging Fruit: The Rate Confirmation
While the gray areas stay open, Naeem sees some fixes as straightforward. The first is the rate confirmation. He described cases in which brokers were sued after shippers added fines to the rate confirmation and the broker delivered that document to the driver. The argument was that the broker, by passing along the penalty, had exercised agency over the driver and pressured the driver to arrive on time.
“Step one has to be auditing what you put on the rate confirmation,” Naeem said. “The rate confirmation is your very first audited document that you are giving to the carrier and the driver, and so ensuring that you strip that of any potential language that might cause adverse behavior, I think is step number one.”
The second step is defining what happens after pickup, including how late loads are documented and how questions and exceptions are escalated.
Automating the Routine, Escalating the Exception
Naeem sees the most technologically advanced brokers moving toward automated communication governed by a documented SOP. Part of the appeal is legal. He described brokers who want to adopt a state-of-the-art system and a detailed SOP, then point to that when something goes wrong. “They want to take responsibility over the SOPs. They do not want to be responsible for the individual to individual communication.”
His guidance is to separate the load lifecycle into stages. Before pickup, brokers should minimize operational burden and automate standard checks, especially confirming that the person arriving at the dock actually works for the assigned carrier. By his estimate, about a third of the brokers he talks with don’t do that today, and the two-thirds who do it manually “open themselves up to even more liability.”
After pickup, he recommends more care. “I.e., a driver is on time, everything checks out with that load. You maybe don’t want someone talking to that person, right? You might want to have it purely automated and let things go.” If the driver replies that something is wrong, the conversation escalates to a human. “I think you’re not going to have a fully agentic solution to this, but I think having agents as a first line of defense to start auditing everything and injecting this information is also really important.”
Call Recording and the Records Problem
On call recording, Naeem has seen both extremes. Some brokers record every call on their VoIP platform and others record none. Selective recording is the approach he cautioned against, saying that choosing not to record conversations with carriers “also looks bad in the court.” His broader point: “ignoring the problem is not the solution.” Any driver can claim a broker said something, he noted, and without a record the broker has little way to respond .
Retention raises its own concerns. Naeem deferred to legal counsel on how long to keep communications, describing his approach as asking chief legal officers how much appetite they have, since more data can support performance analysis. For personally identifiable information, though, his advice was firm: “whenever you’re dealing with PII, you want that destroyed immediately.” He said he has met top 50 brokers with tens of thousands of driver CDLs sitting in email that haven’t been destroyed, each one a hefty potential fine if not destroyed after permitted use.
E3’s approach is to store hashes of driver identities instead of the documents themselves. With about 7,000 drivers verified per day and more than half a million owner-operators seen, Naeem said, the network can recognize a returning driver without the broker collecting a CDL. He also expects some brokers to sunset internal projects that track historical communication data for proprietary on-time metrics, because of the risk of holding records that are incomplete when an incident occurs.
The Shipper Pressure Point
Looking ahead, Naeem sees liability exposure moving up the supply chain. Shippers are paying closer attention to whether their brokers have verification and communication controls in place. He cited the Unilever lawsuit, in which no one checked that the truck arriving at the facility belonged to the intended carrier. After an incident, the shipper became a defendant and, in his words, views the case as a brand risk.
For brokers, he sees an opening rather than a blanket threat. “The brokers who are able to solve this problem, come up with a great solution, are going to have an edge in the market because they’re going to be able to show shippers that hey, I have I have our ship under control,” he said. “I actually think it’s an opportunity for brokers who are active about it.”
No single playbook has emerged on escalation, repowering decisions or AI after pickup, and brokers are making these calls with competing legal and operational risks on both sides. Auditing rate confirmations, tightening SOPs, verifying pickups and minimizing sensitive data are steps within a broker’s control today, and shippers are starting to ask which brokers have taken them.
